section.heading: 2.7. Derivatives and Rates of Change
section.paragraph: Now that we have defined limits and have learned techniques for computing them, we revisit the problems of finding tangent lines and velocities from Section 2.1. The special type of limit that occurs in both of these problems is called a derivative and we will see that it can be interpreted as a rate of change in any of the natural or social sciences or engineering.
section.heading: Tangents
section.paragraph: If a curve $$C$$ has equation $$y = f(x)$$ and we want to find the tangent line to $$C$$ at the point $$P\left( {a,f(a)} \right)$$ , then we consider (as we did in Section 2.1) a nearby point $$Q\left( {x,f(x)} \right)$$ , where $$x \neq a$$ , and compute the slope of the secant line $$PQ$$ :
$$m_{\mathit{PQ}} = \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$$

Then we let $$Q$$ approach $$P$$ along the curve $$C$$ by letting $$x$$ approach $$a$$ . If $$m_{\mathit{PQ}}$$ approaches a number $$m$$ , then we define the tangent line $$\ell$$ to be the line through $$P$$ with slope $$m$$ . (This amounts to saying that the tangent line is the limiting position of the secant line $$\mathit{PQ}$$ as $$Q$$ approaches $$P$$ . See Figure 1.)

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Find an equation of the tangent line to the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ at the point $$P\left( {1,1} \right)$$ .
Solution Here we have $$a = 1$$ and $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ , so the slope is

$$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{f(x) - f(1)}{x - 1} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{2} - 1}{x - 1}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{\left( {x - 1} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right)}{x - 1}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\left( {x + 1} \right) = 1 + 1 = 2}} \end{array}$$

Point-slope form for a line through the point $$\left( x_{1},y_{1} \right)$$ with slope $$m$$ :
$$y - y_{1} = m\left( x - x_{1} \right)$$

section.paragraph: We sometimes refer to the slope of the tangent line to a curve at a point as the slope of the curve at the point. The idea is that if we zoom in far enough toward the point, the curve looks almost like a straight line. Figure 2 illustrates this procedure for the curve $$y = x^{2}$$ in Example 1. The more we zoom in, the more the parabola looks like a line. In other words, the curve becomes almost indistinguishable from its tangent line.

section.paragraph: There is another expression for the slope of a tangent line that is sometimes easier to use. If $$h = x - a$$ , then $$x = a + h$$ and so the slope of the secant line $$\mathit{PQ}$$ is
$$m_{\mathit{PQ}} = \frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}$$
(See Figure 3 where the case $$h > 0$$ is illustrated and $$Q$$ is located to the right of $$P$$ . If it happened that $$h < 0$$ , however, $$Q$$ would be to the left of $$P$$ .)

section.paragraph: Notice that as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ , $$h$$ approaches $$0$$ (because $$h = x - a$$ ) and so the expression for the slope of the tangent line in Definition 1 becomes
$$m = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$$

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find an equation of the tangent line to the hyperbola $$y = 3 \slash x$$ at the point $$\left( {3,1} \right)$$ .

$$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({3 + h})} - f{(3)}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\frac{3}{3 + h} - 1}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\frac{3 - {({3 + h})}}{3 + h}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{- h}{h{({3 + h})}} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0} - \frac{1}{3 + h} = - \frac{1}{3}}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Velocities
section.paragraph: In Section 2.1 we investigated the motion of a ball dropped from the CN Tower and defined its velocity to be the limiting value of average velocities over shorter and shorter time periods.

In general, suppose an object moves along a straight line according to an equation of motion $$s = f(t)$$ , where $$s$$ is the displacement (directed distance) of the object from the origin at time $$t$$ . The function $$f$$ that describes the motion is called the position function of the object. In the time interval from $$t = a$$ to $$t = a + h$$ the change in position is $$f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)$$ . (See Figure 5.)

image.alt: Details A horizontal line labeled s is marked with point 0 on the left end. Two points are marked on the number line to the right of 0 in the irregular intervals: the first point near 0 is labeled position at time t = a; the second point which is far away from 0 is labeled position at time t = a + h. The horizontal distance between 0 and the first marked point is labeled f(a). The horizontal distance between point 0 and the second marked point is labeled f(a + h). The horizontal distance between the first and the second marked points is labeled f(a + h) minus f(a).

section.paragraph: The average velocity over this time interval is
$${average velocity} = \frac{displacement}{time} = \frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}$$
which is the same as the slope of the secant line $$\mathit{PQ}$$ in Figure 6.

section.paragraph: Now suppose we compute the average velocities over shorter and shorter time intervals $$\left\lbrack {a,a + h} \right\rbrack$$ . In other words, we let $$h$$ approach $$0$$ . As in the example of the falling ball, we define the velocity (or instantaneous velocity) $$\upsilon(a)$$ at time $$t = a$$ to be the limit of these average velocities.

Now that we know how to compute limits, let’s reconsider the problem of the falling ball from Example 2.1.3.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Suppose that a ball is dropped from the upper observation deck of the CN Tower, $$450$$ m above the ground.

list.item: (a) What is the velocity of the ball after $$5$$ seconds?
(b) How fast is the ball traveling when it hits the ground?

example.paragraph: Solution Since two different velocities are requested, it’s efficient to start by finding the velocity at a general time $$t = a$$ . Using the equation of motion $$s = f(t) = 4.9t^{2}$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\upsilon{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({a + h})} - f{(a)}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{4.9{({a + h})}^{2} - 4.9a^{2}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{\upsilon{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{4.9{({a^{2} + 2ah + h^{2} - a^{2}})}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{4.9{({2ah + h^{2}})}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{\upsilon{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{4.9h{({2a + h})}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}4.9{({2a + h})} = 9.8a}} \end{array}$$

list.item: (a) The velocity after $$5$$ seconds is $$\upsilon(5) = (9.8)(5) = 49m \slash s$$ .
(b) Since the observation deck is $$450$$ m above the ground, the ball will hit the ground at the time $$t$$ when $$s(t) = 450$$ , that is, $$4.9t^{2} = 450$$

The velocity of the ball as it hits the ground is therefore
$$\upsilon\left( \sqrt{\frac{450}{4.9}} \right) = 9.8\sqrt{\frac{450}{4.9}} \approx 94m \slash s$$

section.heading: Derivatives
section.paragraph: We have seen that the same type of limit arises in finding the slope of a tangent line (Equation 2) or the velocity of an object (Definition 3). In fact, limits of the form
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}$$

arise whenever we calculate a rate of change in any of the sciences or engineering, such as a rate of reaction in chemistry or a marginal cost in economics. Since this type of limit occurs so widely, it is given a special name and notation.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The derivative of a function $$\mathbf{f}$$ at a number $$\mathbf{a}$$ , denoted by $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ , is

section.paragraph: $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ is read “ $$f$$ prime of $$a$$ .”

If we write $$x = a + h$$ , then we have $$h = x - a$$ and $$h$$ approaches $$0$$ if and only if $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ . Therefore an equivalent way of stating the definition of the derivative, as we saw in finding tangent lines (see Definition 1), is
$$f^{\prime}(a) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Use Definition 4 to find the derivative of the function $$f(x) = x^{2} - 8x + 9$$ at the number (a) $$2$$ and (b) $$a$$ .
Solution

list.item: (a) From Definition 4 we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}{(2)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({2 + h})} - f{(2)}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(2)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{{{({2 + h})}^{2} - 8{({2 + h})} + 9} - ( - 3)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(2)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{4 + 4h + h^{2} - 16 - 8h + 9 + 3}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(2)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{h^{2} - 4h}{h} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{h(h - 4)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{(h - 4) = - 4}}}} \end{array}$$

(b) $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({a + h})} - f{(a)}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{{\lbrack{{({a + h})}^{2} - 8{({a + h})} + 9}\rbrack} - {\lbrack{a^{2} - 8a + 9}\rbrack}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{a^{2} + 2ah + h^{2} - 8a - 8h + 9 - a^{2} + 8a - 9}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{2ah + h^{2} - 8h}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{({2a + h - 8}) = {2a - 8}}}} \end{array}$$ As a check on our work in part (a), notice that if we let $$a = 2$$ , then $$f^{\prime}(2) = 2(2) - 8 = - 4$$ .

example.paragraph: Definitions 4 and 5 are equivalent, so we can use either one to compute the derivative. In practice, Definition 4 often leads to simpler computations.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Use Equation 5 to find the derivative of the function $$f(x) = 1/\sqrt{x}$$ at the number $$a(a > 0)$$ .
Solution From Equation 5 we get

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f{(x)} - f{(a)}}{x - a}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}}{x - a} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}}{x - a} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x}\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{x}\sqrt{a}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{\mathit{ax}}(x - a)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{\mathit{ax}}(x - a)} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{x}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{- (x - a)}{\sqrt{\mathit{ax}}(x - a)\left( \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{x} \right)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{- 1}{\sqrt{\mathit{ax}}\left( \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{x} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(a)}} = \frac{- 1}{\sqrt{a^{2}}\left( \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{a} \right)} = \frac{- 1}{a \cdot 2\sqrt{a}} = - \frac{1}{2a^{3/2}}} \end{array}$$
You can verify that using Definition 4 gives the same result.

section.paragraph: We defined the tangent line to the curve $$y = f(x)$$ at the point $$P\left( {a,f(a)} \right)$$ to be the line that passes through $$P$$ and has slope $$m$$ given by Equation 1 or 2. Since, by Definition 4 (and Equation 5), this is the same as the derivative $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ , we can now say the following.
The tangent line to $$y = f(x)$$ at $$\left( {a,f(a)} \right)$$ is the line through $$\left( {a,f(a)} \right)$$ whose slope is equal to $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ , the derivative of $$f$$ at $$a$$ .
If we use the point-slope form of the equation of a line, we can write an equation of the tangent line to the curve $$y = f(x)$$ at the point $$\left( {a,f(a)} \right)$$ :
$$y - f(a) = f^{\prime}(a)\left( {x - a} \right)$$

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Find an equation of the tangent line to the parabola $$y = x^{2} - 8x + 9$$ at the point $$\left( {3, - 6} \right)$$ .

Solution From Example 4(b) we know that the derivative of $$f(x) = x^{2} - 8x + 9$$ at the number $$a$$ is $$f^{\prime}(a) = 2a - 8$$ . Therefore the slope of the tangent line at $$\left( {3, - 6} \right)$$ is $$f^{\prime}(3) = 2(3) - 8 = - 2$$ . Thus an equation of the tangent line, shown in Figure 7, is
$$y - \left( {- 6} \right) = \left( {- 2} \right)\left( {x - 3} \right)$$

section.heading: Rates of Change
section.paragraph: Suppose $$y$$ is a quantity that depends on another quantity $$x$$ . Thus $$y$$ is a function of $$x$$ and we write $$y = f(x)$$ . If $$x$$ changes from $$x_{1}$$ to $$x_{2}$$ , then the change in $$x$$ (also called the increment of $$x$$ ) is
and the corresponding change in $$y$$ is
$$\Delta y = f\left( x_{2} \right) - f\left( x_{1} \right)$$
The difference quotient
$$\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \frac{f\left( x_{2} \right) - f\left( x_{1} \right)}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$

is called the average rate of change of $$\mathbf{y}$$ with respect to $$\mathbf{x}$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{1},x_{2}} \right\rbrack$$ and can be interpreted as the slope of the secant line $$\mathit{PQ}$$ in Figure 8.

image.alt: Details A curve, a secant line, and a tangent line are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed with tick marks x_1 and x_2, in the order from left to right. The curve enters above the x axis, goes up and to the right through a labeled point P(x_1, f(x_1)), concave down, and then passes through another labeled point Q(x_2, f(x_2)) before reaching its high point. Vertical line segments from points P and Q are dropped to the x axis, meeting it at tick marks x_1 and x_2, respectively. The horizontal distance between the points P and Q is represented by a horizontal segment and is labeled Delta x. The vertical distance between the points P and Q is represented by a vertical segment and is labeled Delta y. The secant line with a positive slope enters above the x axis, goes up and to the right, and intersects the curve at two labeled points P and Q, thus forming a right triangle with base Delta x and height Delta y. The tangent line with a positive slope enters below the secant line and above the curve, goes up and to the right, and intersects the curve exactly once at the marked point P(x_1, f(x_1)). The text below reads, an average rate of change = m_(P Q); instantaneous rate of change = slope of the tangent at P.

figure.caption: $${average rate of change} = m_{\mathit{PQ}}$$ $${instantaneous rate of change} = {slope of tangent at}P$$

section.paragraph: By analogy with velocity, we consider the average rate of change over smaller and smaller intervals by letting $$x_{2}$$ approach $$x_{1}$$ and therefore letting $$\Delta x$$ approach $$0$$ . The limit of these average rates of change is called the (instantaneous) rate of change of $$\mathbf{y}$$ with respect to $$\mathbf{x}$$ at $$x = x_{1}$$ , which (as in the case of velocity) is interpreted as the slope of the tangent to the curve $$y = f(x)$$ at $$P\left( {x_{1},f\left( x_{1} \right)} \right)$$ :
$${instantaneous rate of change} = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \lim\limits_{x_{2}\rightarrow x_{1}}\frac{f(x_{2}) - f(x_{1})}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$$
We recognize this limit as being the derivative $$f^{\prime}\left( x_{1} \right)$$ .
We know that one interpretation of the derivative $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ is as the slope of the tangent line to the curve $$y = f(x)$$ when $$x = a$$ . We now have a second interpretation:
The derivative $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ is the instantaneous rate of change of $$y = f(x)$$ with respect to $$x$$ when $$x = a$$ .

The connection with the first interpretation is that if we sketch the curve $$y = f(x)$$ , then the instantaneous rate of change is the slope of the tangent to this curve at the point where $$x = a$$ . This means that when the derivative is large (and therefore the curve is steep, as at the point $$P$$ in Figure 9), the $$y$$ -values change rapidly. When the derivative is small, the curve is relatively flat (as at point $$Q$$ ) and the $$y$$ -values change slowly.

image.alt: Details A curve with two tangents is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve enters the third quadrant, goes up and to the right through a labeled point P, concaves down, and then passes through another labeled point Q before reaching its high point. Two tangent lines with a positive slope are drawn above the curve. The first tangent line enters the third quadrant, goes upward to the right, and intersects the curve exactly once at the labeled point P. The second tangent line enters the second quadrant, goes up and to the right, not as steep as the first tangent line, but intersects the curve exactly once at the labeled point Q.

figure.caption: The $$y$$ -values are changing rapidly at $$P$$ and slowly at $$Q$$ .

section.paragraph: In particular, if $$s = f(t)$$ is the position function of a particle that moves along a straight line, then $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ is the rate of change of the displacement $$s$$ with respect to the time $$t$$ . In other words, $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ is the velocity of the particle at time $$t = a$$ . The speed of the particle is the absolute value of the velocity, that is, $$\left| f^{\prime}(a) \right|$$ .
In the next example we discuss the meaning of the derivative of a function that is defined verbally.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: A manufacturer produces bolts of a fabric with a fixed width. The cost of producing $$x$$ yards of this fabric is $$C = f(x)$$ dollars.

list.item: (a) What is the meaning of the derivative $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ ? What are its units?
(b) In practical terms, what does it mean to say that $$f^{\prime}(1000) = 9$$ ?
(c) Which do you think is greater, $$f^{\prime}(50)$$ or $$f^{\prime}(500)$$ ? What about $$f^{\prime}(5000)$$ ?

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) The derivative $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is the instantaneous rate of change of $$C$$ with respect to $$x$$ ; that is, $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ means the rate of change of the production cost with respect to the number of yards produced. (Economists call this rate of change the marginal cost. This idea is discussed in more detail in Sections 3.7 and 4.7.) Because $$f^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta C}{\Delta x}$$ the units for $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ are the same as the units for the difference quotient $$\Delta C \slash \Delta x$$ . Since $$\Delta C$$ is measured in dollars and $$\Delta x$$ in yards, it follows that the units for $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ are dollars per yard.

(b) The statement that $$f^{\prime}(1000) = 9$$ means that, after $$1000$$ yards of fabric have been manufactured, the rate at which the production cost is increasing is $$\$ 9 \slash {yard}$$ . (When $$x = 1000$$ , $$C$$ is increasing $$9$$ times as fast as $$x$$ .) Since $$\Delta x = 1$$ is small compared with $$x = 1000$$ , we could use the approximation $$f^{\prime}(1000) \approx \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta x} = \frac{\Delta C}{1} = \Delta C$$ and say that the cost of manufacturing the $$1000$$ th yard (or the $$1001$$ st) is about $$\$ 9$$ . Here we are assuming that the cost function is well behaved; in other words, $$C(x)$$ doesn’t oscillate rapidly near $$x = 1000$$ .

(c) The rate at which the production cost is increasing (per yard) is probably lower when $$x = 500$$ than when $$x = 50$$ (the cost of making the $$500$$ th yard is less than the cost of the $$50$$ th yard) because of economies of scale. (The manufacturer makes more efficient use of the fixed costs of production.) So $$f^{\prime}(50) > f^{\prime}(500)$$ But, as production expands, the resulting large-scale operation might become inefficient and there might be overtime costs. Thus it is possible that the rate of increase of costs will eventually start to rise. So it may happen that $$f^{\prime}(5000) > f^{\prime}(500)$$

section.paragraph: In the following example we estimate the rate of change of the national debt with respect to time. Here the function is defined not by a formula but by a table of values.

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Let $$D(t)$$ be the US national debt at time $$t$$ . The table below gives approximate values of this function by providing end of year estimates, in billions of dollars, from 2000 to 2016. Interpret and estimate the value of $$D^{\prime}(2008)$$ .
Solution The derivative $$D^{\prime}(2008)$$ means the rate of change of $$D$$ with respect to $$t$$ when $$t = 2008$$ , that is, the rate of increase of the national debt in $$2008$$ .
According to Equation 5,
$$D^{\prime}(2008) = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 2008}\frac{D(t) - D(2008)}{t - 2008}$$
One way we can estimate this value is to compare average rates of change over different time intervals by computing difference quotients, as compiled in the following table.

From this table we see that $$D^{\prime}(2008)$$ lies somewhere between $$775.93$$ and $$1433.23$$ billion dollars per year. [Here we are making the reasonable assumption that the debt didn’t fluctuate wildly between 2004 and 2012.] A good estimate for the rate of increase of the US national debt in 2008 would be the average of these two numbers, namely
$$D^{\prime}(2008) \approx 1105{billion dollars}{per year}$$
Another method would be to plot the debt function and estimate the slope of the tangent line when $$t = 2008$$ .

note.title: A Note on Units
note.heading: A Note on Units
note.paragraph: The units for the average rate of change $$\Delta D \slash \Delta t$$ are the units for $$\Delta D$$ divided by the units for $$\Delta t$$ , namely billions of dollars per year. The instantaneous rate of change is the limit of the average rates of change, so it is measured in the same units: billions of dollars per year.

section.paragraph: In Examples 3, 7, and 8 we saw three specific examples of rates of change: the velocity of an object is the rate of change of displacement with respect to time; marginal cost is the rate of change of production cost with respect to the number of items produced; the rate of change of the debt with respect to time is of interest in economics. Here is a small sample of other rates of change: In physics, the rate of change of work with respect to time is called power. Chemists who study a chemical reaction are interested in the rate of change in the concentration of a reactant with respect to time (called the rate of reaction). A biologist is interested in the rate of change of the population of a colony of bacteria with respect to time. In fact, the computation of rates of change is important in all of the natural sciences, in engineering, and even in the social sciences. Further examples will be given in Section 3.7.

All these rates of change are derivatives and can therefore be interpreted as slopes of tangents. This gives added significance to the solution of the tangent problem. Whenever we solve a problem involving tangent lines, we are not just solving a problem in geometry. We are also implicitly solving a great variety of problems involving rates of change in science and engineering.
section.heading: Writing Project Early Methods for Finding Tangents
section.paragraph: The first person to explicitly formulate the ideas of limits and derivatives was Sir Isaac Newton in the 1660s. But Newton acknowledged that “If I have seen further than other men, it is because I have stood on the shoulders of giants.” Two of those giants were Pierre Fermat (1601–1665) and Newton’s mentor at Cambridge, Isaac Barrow (1630–1677). Newton was familiar with the methods that these men used to find tangent lines, and their methods played a role in Newton’s eventual formulation of calculus.

Learn about these methods by researching on the Internet or reading one of the references listed here. Write an essay comparing the methods of either Fermat or Barrow to modern methods. In particular, use the method of Section 2.7 to find an equation of the tangent line to the curve $$y = x^{3} + 2x$$ at the point $$(1,3)$$ and show how either Fermat or Barrow would have solved the same problem. Although you used derivatives and they did not, point out similarities between the methods.
